title: The Supply Side of School Choice: Who participates? Who doesn't?
author: Michael McShane
summary: Michael McShane of EdChoice examines a new peer-reviewed study by Matthew Lee, Benjamin Scafidi, Roger Tutterow, and Damian Kavanagh on why private schools do or don't participate in school-choice programs. Drawing on a survey of 473 private school leaders, the study finds religious schools, schools in the northeastern U.S., and schools serving special-needs students participate at meaningfully higher rates, while schools with tuition above $20,000 and schools under 250 students participate at lower rates. McShane highlights a surprising finding: among participating schools, 40 percent waited an average of 7.35 years after a program launched before joining, a delay he says is worth investigating further. He frames the findings through a Milton Friedman lens, that organizations respond to incentives, and argues for his long-standing preference for sliding-scale ESA funding tied to student need, similar to Arizona's approach, as a way to expand the range of schools willing to participate.
points: A new survey-based study of 473 private school leaders finds religious schools, schools in the northeastern U.S., and special-needs-focused schools participate in choice programs at significantly higher rates.
Schools with tuition above $20,000 and schools serving fewer than 250 students are significantly less likely to participate in choice programs.
Among schools that do participate, 40 percent waited an average of 7.35 years after program launch to join, a delay McShane calls the study's most surprising and least-explained finding.

McShane argues, invoking Milton Friedman, that school participation is fundamentally a response to incentives: schools join when the funding covers their costs and serves the students they're built to serve.
He restates his longstanding preference for sliding-scale ESA funding (more money for higher student need), pointing to Arizona's disability plus-up model as an example already in practice.
quotes: If you build it, they will come makes a great tagline for a mythical baseball movie but a poor strategy for educational improvement.
Markets are not magic and are shaped by external factors that encourage or discourage participation.
Private schools with tuitions above $20,000 are 33 points less likely to participate than schools with tuitions below $20,000
I was surprised at the mean time schools waited to participate in choice programs.
What became apparent in year seven that wasn’t clear in year six or year five? That one is worth thinking about and trying to unpack.
I imagine he would tell me that organizations respond to incentives. If they get enough money to cover their tuition costs, they’ll participate in the program.
But regardless of my half-baked thoughts, this was an interesting and thought-provoking paper that everyone should check out.
